title: RL Transient: Why an Inductor Slows the Current
topic: Series RL transient — when the switch closes, current rises along i(t) = (V/R)(1 - e^{-t/τ}) with τ = L/R, because the inductor opposes any change in current and develops a back-emf that decays as the current settles.

beats.narration: Flip a switch onto an inductor — and the current refuses to jump. What's stopping it?

elements.content: Manimo bobs in centre-screen
Switch closes — but the current eases in. Why?

beats.narration: Battery V in series with a resistor R and an inductor L. Close the switch — current starts to rise, but the inductor pushes back.

elements.content: Rectangular loop wire
Battery on left vertical with V label
Switch on top wire, opens then rotates closed
Resistor zigzag on right vertical upper
Inductor coil (4 humps) on right vertical lower
Back-emf arrow on the inductor opposing current
the inductor opposes any change in current

beats.narration: The current rises along an exponential curve toward V over R, while the voltage across the inductor decays from V down to zero — perfect mirror images.

elements.content: Time axis with i(t) and V_L(t) on same chart
i(t) = (V/R)(1 - e^{-t/τ}) — rises from 0 toward V/R, amber
V_L(t) = V·e^{-t/τ} — decays from V toward 0, rose
time cursor sweeping across

beats.narration: Tau equals L over R is the time constant. After one tau the current has reached sixty three percent of its final value. After five tau it is essentially full.

elements.content: τ = L/R
i(t) curve with τ marker (63%) and 5τ marker (~99%)
τ marker — vertical dashed line plus dot at 63% of V/R
5τ marker — vertical dashed line plus dot at ~99% of V/R
one τ → 63%   ·   five τ → essentially full

beats.narration: Bigger L slows the rise; bigger R hurries it. The time constant L over R sets the rhythm — the exact opposite trade-off from R C.

elements.content: Bigger L → slower rise.  Bigger R → faster rise.
τ = L/R sets the rhythm.
